a: The Song of Songs, the best of songs
p: The Hebrew form means the finest of all songs, as 'holy of holies' means the holiest place.
b: Shir hashirim is a superlative: a word repeated in the plural to mean 'the best of its kind', like 'holy of holies' (Exodus 26:33) or 'king of kings' (Ezekiel 26:7). It does not mean a song made of songs. Most readers take it as a boast by the editor: of all the songs credited to Solomon (1 Kings 4:32 says he wrote 1,005), this is the best. Jewish tradition took the title as a claim about the book's rank among the Writings (see the opening pages of this book).
orig: שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים (shir hashirim), 'song of the songs'
r: Exodus 26:33; Ezekiel 26:7; 1 Kings 4:32

a: of Solomon
p: The little Hebrew word 'of' can mean by, for, about, or in the style of Solomon.
b: Lishlomo is the preposition le plus Solomon's name. In Hebrew titles le can mean 'by' (Psalm 3:0 'of David'), 'for', 'about', or 'belonging to the collection of'. The text names Solomon again at 1:5; 3:7, 9, 11 and 8:11, 12, seven times in all, and in 8:12 the woman sets 'my own vineyard' beside his, so he may be the lover, a stock figure of royal luxury, or a foil. First Kings 4:32 credits him with 1,005 songs, and Sirach 47:14-17 praises his songs and riddles. Whether he wrote this one is argued in the opening pages of this book.
r: 1 Kings 4:32; 1 Kings 11:1–3; Psalm 72:0; Sirach 47:14–17; Song of Songs 8:12

a: Your lovemaking is better than wine
p: Wine is the Song's first picture of love: sweet, strong, and shared.
b: Love and wine are paired again at 1:4, 4:10 and 7:9, and 5:1 asks the friends to 'drink and be drunk'. Wine here pictures a pleasure that goes to the head; it is not a hint about drinking. The Hebrew also turns from 'him' (1:2a) to 'you' (1:2b) in one breath: the woman speaks of her lover and then to him. Some translations smooth this out. The shift marks how the whole Song talks, with the lover sometimes present and sometimes only imagined.
r: Song of Songs 1:4; Song of Songs 4:10; Song of Songs 5:1; Song of Songs 7:9; Proverbs 5:19; Psalm 104:15

a: oil emptied out
p: The Hebrew sounds like 'oil' and 'name'; the oil is 'emptied' or 'poured out'.
b: Shemen (oil) and shem (name) sound alike, and the line plays on that. 'Emptied out' (turaq) is a rare form; most take it as 'poured out', so that the name's scent spreads. In the ancient world a name meant a person's reputation, and a good scent marked someone worth meeting. The point is that his name alone is enough to arouse her.

a: young women
p: The Hebrew 'alamot' means young women of marrying age; it does not say whether they are virgins.
b: 'Alamot are young women of marrying age. The word does not itself say they have never had sex (Proverbs 30:19 uses it for 'the way of a man with a young woman', which is not about virginity). Older English versions often wrote 'virgins'. The same root lies behind Isaiah 7:14, a separate debate that is taken up there. Here the young women love him for his name alone.
r: Proverbs 30:19; Psalm 68:25; Isaiah 7:14

a: The king has taken me into his private rooms
p: The 'king' may be Solomon, the lover called king in love-talk, or God.
b: Four readings. (1) The lover is Solomon, and she is taken into the royal harem. (2) He is an ordinary man spoken of as a king, as at village weddings in Syria where, in the nineteenth century, the groom and bride were called king and queen for the wedding week (Wetzstein, 1873). (3) He is a royal figure of her daydream. (4) In the old allegories the king is God (the Targum) or Christ (Origen), and the 'rooms' are the inner places of prayer and knowledge.
r: Song of Songs 3:9; Song of Songs 3:11; Song of Songs 7:5; Psalm 45:13–15

a: I am dark, and I am lovely
p: The Hebrew has 'and', not 'but': her dark skin and her loveliness are not set against each other.
b: The Hebrew letter waw is 'and'. Many English versions, following the Latin nigra sum sed formosa, write 'dark but lovely', which makes her skin a problem to be overcome. The Hebrew says nothing like that. The next verse gives the reason she is dark: the sun has looked at her while she worked outdoors. Her brothers' scorn (1:6) is part of the pain, but she does not apologize for her color. Both things are true at once.
r: Song of Songs 1:6; Lamentations 4:8; Job 30:30

a: the tents of Kedar
p: Kedar was an Arabian tribe whose tents of dark goat hair stood for desert life.
b: Kedar was a nomadic Arab people, descended from Ishmael in Genesis 25:13, who lived in the desert east and south of Israel and are linked to tents of black goat hair (Psalm 120:5; Isaiah 21:16–17; Jeremiah 49:28–29). She is dark like those tents, and as beautiful as they are as a shelter in the desert. Then 'like the tent curtains of Solomon' sets beside them the finest hangings of the king. Some scholars read the Hebrew Shelomoh here as another Arab name, Shalmah; most keep Solomon.
r: Genesis 25:13; Psalm 120:5; Isaiah 21:16–17; Jeremiah 49:28–29; Exodus 26:7

a: My mother's sons
p: The woman speaks of her mother's household. Mothers appear in the Song; fathers never do.
b: 'My mother's sons' are her brothers, but the phrase leaves out the father. In the Song a mother is named in 1:6; 3:4, 11; 6:9; 8:1, 2, 5 and a father never is. Carol Meyers takes this as a sign that the poems come from the women's world of the 'mother's house', where a young woman's first plans for love and marriage were made (compare Genesis 24:28; Ruth 1:8). The brothers' anger comes back in 8:8–9, where they plan for their little sister.
r: Song of Songs 3:4; Song of Songs 8:1; Song of Songs 8:8–9; Genesis 24:28; Ruth 1:8

a: guard of the vineyards
p: Her own vineyard is probably herself, which her brothers gave her no time to tend.
b: 'Vineyard' (kerem) is a lover's word in this Song. In 2:15 the vineyards are in bloom, and in 8:11–12 the woman holds up 'my own vineyard' against Solomon's. Most readers take her vineyard as herself, or her body and her freedom to love: her brothers set her to work on their land, and she had no time for her own. Isaiah 5:1–7 sings of 'my beloved' and his vineyard, which stands for Israel, so the image was a familiar one for a loved person or people. The woman comes back to the idea in the last chapter.
r: Song of Songs 2:15; Song of Songs 8:11–12; Isaiah 5:1–7; Hosea 14:7

a: you whom I love with my whole self
p: 'Nefesh' means life, self, throat and desire; it is not a soul apart from the body.
b: The woman calls her lover 'the one my nefesh loves' here and in 3:1–4. Nefesh is not the spirit separate from the body, as 'soul' often suggests today. In the Bible it is the whole living self, the throat that eats and drinks, and the appetite that wants. The Plain English Translation says 'with my whole self' every time. The Hebrew phrase is the same in each place, and in 3:1–4 its repetition ties together the whole night search.
r: Song of Songs 3:1–4; Deuteronomy 6:5; Psalm 42:1–2

a: If you do not know
p: Whose voice answers: the daughters, the lover in disguise, or her own thought?
b: The question of 1:7 is answered in 1:8, but not by anyone named. 'Beautiful one among women' (also 5:9; 6:1) is how others address her, so many take the answer to come from the daughters of Jerusalem, teasing: if you do not know where he is, follow the tracks of the flock and look among the shepherds' tents. Others hear the lover himself, playing a shepherd. A few hear the woman's own reflection. In allegory the voice is the Church, or God, telling the soul to follow the footsteps of the saints.
r: Song of Songs 5:9; Song of Songs 6:1; Genesis 29:1–10

a: I compare you to my mare
p: Egyptian chariot teams were stallions, so a mare among them would stir them up.
b: Egyptian war chariots were drawn by stallions, and Marvin Pope pointed out that a mare in the harness would drive them wild. If so, the man praises her as a beauty who throws everyone off balance. The Greek poet Theocritus (about 270 BC) compares Helen to a horse of Thessaly in a chariot team (Idyll 18), a comparison from a different world. Solomon imported horses and chariots from Egypt (1 Kings 10:28–29), so Pharaoh's chariots were the finest of their day. The comparison does not call her an animal: it says she is sleek, dazzling and strong.
r: 1 Kings 10:28–29; Exodus 14:6–7; Isaiah 31:1

a: We will make you jewelry of gold
p: The plural 'we' may be the man and his friends, the daughters, or a royal 'we'.
b: The speaker of 1:9–11 is a man, since he calls her 'my darling'. The 'we' is then a surprise. It may be the lover speaking for himself and his companions, as the chorus does in 1:4. It may be a plural of generosity. Or a group (the daughters of Jerusalem) may be speaking for him. Gold ornaments with silver studs are the kind of gift given at a wedding, and since he says he will make them, they are a promise and not a present. Gold and silver also make up Solomon's litter in 3:9–10.
r: Song of Songs 3:10; Genesis 24:22; Genesis 24:53; Ezekiel 16:11–13

a: nard
p: Nard was a costly perfume brought from India or Nepal.
b: Nerd is spikenard (Nardostachys jatamansi), a plant of the Himalayas whose root was ground into an oil. It came thousands of miles along the spice routes, so a flask of it was very costly. In John 12:3 Mary of Bethany pours a pound of pure nard on Jesus' feet, and Judas puts its worth at 300 denarii (John 12:5), about a laborer's pay for a year. The word itself is thought to come from the Sanskrit nalada, one of the Song's foreign words. Here the woman's nard fills the room as the king reclines at his couch.
r: Song of Songs 4:13–14; John 12:3–5; Mark 14:3

a: A pouch of myrrh
p: Myrrh is a sweet resin from Arabia; the verse pictures him resting all night against her.
b: Myrrh (mor) is a resin from the bark of an Arabian tree, used in perfume, in the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:23) and in the year of beauty treatments that Esther received (Esther 2:12). It appears in the Song more than in any other book (1:13; 3:6; 4:6, 14; 5:1, 5, 13). Proverbs 7:17 shows the foreign woman perfuming her bed with myrrh, aloes and cinnamon, the same scents the Song uses of a loving couple: the spices are not wicked in themselves. The 'pouch' is a small bag on a cord, so 'between my breasts' means it rests over her heart.
r: Exodus 30:23; Esther 2:12; Proverbs 7:17; Psalm 45:8

a: henna blossoms
p: Henna (kofer) is a shrub with sweet-smelling clusters of flowers. En-gedi is an oasis by the Dead Sea.
b: Kofer is henna (Lawsonia inermis), a bush with clusters of small, strongly scented flowers whose leaves give the orange-red dye used on hands and hair. The word also means 'ransom' in other places, but here it is the plant. En-gedi ('spring of the young goat') is an oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 24:1). A vineyard of henna in that dry cliff country would be a burst of green and scent in the desert.
r: 1 Samuel 24:1; Song of Songs 4:13; Joshua 15:62

a: Your eyes are doves
p: The comparison is about how the eyes feel and move, not their shape.
b: The Song's pictures give an impression and not an outline. A dove's eye is bright and soft, doves come in pairs, and they move quickly and gently. The man calls her 'my dove' in 2:14, 5:2 and 6:9, and he is given the same doves' eyes in 5:12. Fox notes that such pictures say how she strikes him and not what she looks like, which is why the verses never add up to a drawing. The Egyptian love songs use birds in the same way.
r: Song of Songs 2:14; Song of Songs 4:1; Song of Songs 5:12; Song of Songs 5:2

a: Our bed is fresh and green
p: The 'green bed' puts the lovers in a leafy outdoor place, in a house of trees.
b: The Hebrew ra'ananah is the word for a living tree's fresh green (Psalm 92:14; Jeremiah 11:16). The couple's bed (eres) is green with leaves, and 1:17 says their house is cedar and cypress, the trees of Lebanon. Many readers have found the lovers in a bower of trees. Others take it as a way to say that their love is fresh and flourishing.
r: Psalm 92:14; Jeremiah 11:16; Song of Songs 1:17; Hosea 14:8

a: Cedars are the beams of our house
p: The beams and rafters are the finest timber; the 'house' may be a bower.
b: Cedar and cypress (or juniper) were the costly timbers of Solomon's palace and temple (1 Kings 5:8; 6:15; 7:2). Two details in the Hebrew: 'houses' is plural, as if the whole outdoors were their home, and the word for 'rafters' is written one way and read another (a chet or a he), which is a spelling difference and not a different word. A lovers' hut of trees has the luxury of a palace.
r: 1 Kings 5:8; 1 Kings 6:15; 1 Kings 7:2

a: I am a crocus of the Sharon plain
t: The 'rose of Sharon' and who is speaking
p: The woman speaks here, not Christ. The flower is a crocus or similar bulb; 'rose' is the English translators' word.
b: Chavatselet is a rare word for a flower of the meadows (it appears again only in Isaiah 35:1). It is probably a crocus, a narcissus or an asphodel, a small bulb flower that blooms in the spring. The Greek has 'flower of the plain' (anthos tou pediou) and the Latin Vulgate 'flower of the field' (flos campi), not a rose. The 'rose of Sharon' comes from the King James Version, and hymns like 'Lily of the Valley' and sermons that make Jesus say 'I am the rose of Sharon' take the line as Christ's own. In the Hebrew the speaker is the woman: the man answers in 2:2 with 'my darling'. Her modesty is part of the point. Sharon is the coastal plain, a wide grassland; Isaiah 33:9 mourns that it has become 'like the desert plain'.
r: Isaiah 35:1; Isaiah 33:9; Song of Songs 2:2

a: A lily among thorns
p: The man answers: she is as rare among other girls as a lily among thorns.
b: The man takes up her word 'lily' (shoshannah, probably the water lily or lotus of Egypt, or the wild lily of the fields; it appears eight times in the Song) and says she is a lily among thorns. 'The daughters' are the other young women. Christian readers from the early centuries read the lily as the Church among the thorns of persecution, and the rabbis read it as Israel among the nations. In Egyptian love songs a girl is often 'the one' beside whom all others are nothing.
r: Song of Songs 2:16; Song of Songs 4:5; Song of Songs 6:2–3; Hosea 14:5

a: An apple tree
p: The Hebrew 'tappuach' names a sweet, scented tree fruit; which fruit is unknown.
b: Tappuach appears here and in 2:5, 7:8 and 8:5 (and in Joel 1:12, Proverbs 25:11). The fruit is round and golden in Proverbs 25:11, sweet and scented in the Song, and grows on a tree with shade. Apples as we know them were rare in the ancient Middle East, and the apricot, quince, citron and even the pomegranate have all been proposed. 'Apple' is the English tradition. The Plain English Translation says 'apple tree' and 'apples' and leaves the botany open. The exact fruit matters less than what the verse says: she sits in his shade and finds his fruit sweet.
r: Song of Songs 2:5; Song of Songs 7:8; Song of Songs 8:5; Proverbs 25:11; Joel 1:12

a: the house of wine
p: 'House of wine' is a feasting hall, with a wedding feast in the background.
b: The Hebrew bet hayayin occurs only here. It is the feasting house, like the 'house of feasting' of Jeremiah 16:8 and Ecclesiastes 7:2, where wine flowed. The setting may be a real wedding banquet, or the image may stand for the whole experience of love as a feast. Some old readers took it as the place of the Law and the Church's table, and the bridal chamber as the Church's inner life.
r: Jeremiah 16:8; Ecclesiastes 7:2; Esther 7:8; Song of Songs 5:1

a: love is his banner over me
p: 'Degel' means a banner or military flag. Some link it to a look; the Latin Vulgate reads 'he set love in order in me'.
b: Degel is a banner or standard, the flag each tribe raised in the camp (Numbers 2:2). In the Song the word comes again only in 6:4, 10 (the 'troops with banners'). The picture is that he marks her as his and the banner says 'love'. The English chorus 'His banner over me is love' follows this 'banner' reading. Some scholars link degel to the Akkadian dagalu, 'to look', and read 'his look at me was love'. The Latin Vulgate reads differently again: ordinavit in me caritatem, 'he set love in order in me'.
r: Numbers 2:2; Song of Songs 6:4; Song of Songs 6:10

a: raisin cakes
p: Cakes of pressed raisins were festive food, also eaten in the worship of other gods.
b: Ashishot are cakes of pressed raisins, a sweet and energizing food. David gave them to the crowd as the ark came to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:19; 1 Chronicles 16:3). In Hosea 3:1 Israel loves 'raisin cakes' offered to other gods, so they could be cult food as well. Here they are a lovers' fortifier: she asks for the sweets that revive her when she faints from desire.
r: 2 Samuel 6:19; 1 Chronicles 16:3; Hosea 3:1

a: for love has made me sick
p: Love as a sickness is known in Egyptian songs and in the Bible's story of Amnon.
b: The Hebrew says cholat ahavah ani, 'sick of love am I', and uses it again in 5:8. Egyptian love songs also speak of lovesickness, including a lover who has gone days without seeing the beloved and falls ill (Fox collects them, with Papyrus Chester Beatty I). In 2 Samuel 13:2 Amnon makes himself sick for Tamar, with an ugly end. The word in the Song is not shame but a faint, a longing that weakens the knees. The cure is food and an embrace.
r: Song of Songs 5:8; 2 Samuel 13:2

a: do not wake love and do not stir it up / until it wants to
p: She makes the daughters swear not to rouse love before it is ready. The views differ on what 'not rousing' means.
b: The same charge returns at 3:5 and 8:4, and its form is an oath: 'if you wake...' in the Hebrew is the old way of saying 'you will not'. Views. (1) Do not hurry love: let it come in its own time, a warning to girls about haste before marriage. (2) Do not interrupt a couple who are in love, while they lie in each other's arms (see 2:6, 3:5 and 8:3). (3) Do not force love by drugs, magic or pressure. (4) In Jewish tradition, God makes Israel swear not to rebel against the nations or force the end (Song of Songs Rabbah; Babylonian Talmud, Ketubbot 111a). (5) Christian writers took it as a charge to leave the Bridegroom's rest alone. The refrain closes each of the book's three cycles. The Hebrew of 8:4 differs a little (see there).
r: Song of Songs 3:5; Song of Songs 8:4; Song of Songs 5:8

a: by the gazelles or by the does of the field
p: The oath avoids God's name and swears by animals; the Hebrew sounds like 'armies' and 'God Almighty'.
b: Oaths were sworn by God (Genesis 21:23). Here the woman swears by tseva'ot ('gazelles') and ayyelot hassadeh ('does of the field'). The words sound like tseva'ot ('armies', as in 'the LORD of Armies') and El Shaddai ('God Almighty'), so the rabbis heard a hidden oath by God, and the Song then uses God's name without using it. Fox and others doubt any such intent and think the animals are swift, shy things that stand for love itself, which also must not be startled. Both could be true. The Septuagint did not translate the animals at all: Swete's Codex Vaticanus has 'by the powers and by the forces of the field' here and at 3:5 (see the variant), which suggests that its translators also heard 'armies' and 'strength' in the Hebrew words.
r: Genesis 21:23; 1 Samuel 1:3; Genesis 17:1

a: springing over the mountains
p: The rabbis heard God leaping over the mountains of time to free Israel from Egypt.
b: Song of Songs Rabbah reads the lover's springing over the mountains as God's swift coming to redeem his people, and the synagogue reads the whole Song at Passover, in the spring. The verses about winter and spring in 2:11–13 make the match easy, since Passover falls at the start of spring. Christian readers heard the same leap as the Word's coming down to earth, from heaven to womb to cross. In the plain sense it is a picture of the lover's speed and joy.
r: Exodus 12:1–14; Song of Songs 2:11–13; Song of Songs 2:17

a: a gazelle or a young deer
p: The lover is swift, graceful and shy, like the animals of the hills.
b: The gazelle (tsevi) is a small, fast antelope of the hills and plains, and the 'young deer' (ofer ha'ayyalim) is the young of the deer. The couple use both again at 2:17 and 8:14, and the woman's breasts are likened to fawns (4:5; 7:3). They stand for speed, shyness and beauty; a man 'like a gazelle' was also praised for fast running in war (2 Samuel 2:18; 1 Chronicles 12:8). The lover stands 'behind our wall', looking in at the windows and peering through the lattice, so the barrier between them is part of the longing.
r: Song of Songs 2:17; Song of Songs 8:14; 2 Samuel 2:18; 1 Chronicles 12:8; Proverbs 5:19

a: Get up, my darling, my beautiful one
p: The woman's call 'lekhi lakh' sounds like God's call to Abram, 'lekh lekha' (Genesis 12:1).
b: The invitation of 2:10 and 2:13 uses a pair of words, lekhi lakh, 'go for yourself', the feminine of lekh lekha, God's call to Abram to leave his land (Genesis 12:1). It was used again for Abraham with Isaac (Genesis 22:2). In 2:13 the word lakh is written lekhi (the Ketiv, 'what is written') and read lakh (the Qere, 'what is read aloud'), a small spelling change. Whether the echo is intended is not known. The Song may be playing on the language of a call that begins a journey.
orig: קוּמִי לָךְ רַעְיָתִי יָפָתִי וּלְכִי לָךְ
r: Genesis 12:1; Genesis 22:2; Song of Songs 2:13

a: the winter has passed
p: In Israel 'winter' means the rainy months, ending in March; spring flowers appear at once.
b: The Hebrew setav is the rainy winter, which runs from about October to March in Israel. When the rains stop, the hills turn green in a few weeks and wildflowers cover them; figs and vines put out leaves and buds (2:13). The Ketiv spells the word without a yod, which is only a difference in spelling. The Passover is in this season, and the rabbis read the Song at Passover for that reason.
r: Song of Songs 2:12–13; Deuteronomy 11:14; Exodus 12:2

a: The time for pruning has come
p: The Hebrew 'zamir' can mean pruning (as the vines need) or singing (as the birds do).
b: Zamir comes from a root that means both 'to sing' (zimrah, 'song') and 'to prune' (Leviticus 25:3-4; Isaiah 18:5). Modern versions mostly choose 'singing', because the line stands beside the dove's voice. The ancient translators chose pruning: the Greek has 'time of cutting' and the Latin Vulgate has putationis, 'of pruning'. The Plain English Translation follows pruning, because the vines are the subject in 2:13 and the cutting of vines is the work of the spring; but the double meaning is probably intended, and the verse offers both.
r: Leviticus 25:3–4; Isaiah 18:5; Song of Songs 2:13

a: in the clefts of the rock
p: The dove hides in a rock; Jewish and Christian readers found Israel at the sea or the Church in Christ's wounds.
b: A rock dove nests in the cliffs, so the picture is of a shy woman who keeps out of sight. The man asks her to show herself and to speak. The Targum has Israel at the Red Sea, hemmed in between Pharaoh's army and the water, like a dove in the clefts of the rock. Bernard of Clairvaux (Sermon 61) took the clefts as the wounds of Christ in which the soul finds shelter, and the English hymn 'Rock of Ages, cleft for me' comes from that kind of reading, with Exodus 33:22 behind it. The Hebrew says nothing of the kind: the man just wants to see and hear her.
r: Exodus 33:22; Isaiah 32:2; Jeremiah 48:28; Song of Songs 5:2

a: Seize the foxes for us
p: The foxes ruin the vineyards; they may be pests, rivals, temptations or enemies, and the speaker is unclear.
b: Five readings. (1) Real foxes or jackals that dig up the vines and eat the grapes, so that this is a vineyard worker's song. (2) A work song or riddle sung by the brothers or the daughters, a request that the couple help guard the vines. (3) Young men who spoil a girl's chances, or lovers who 'trample' a vineyard (here the vineyard stands for the woman, as in 1:6), so the foxes are threats to love. (4) In Origen and Augustine, heretics who spoil the Church; in Bernard, little vices and temptations. (5) In the Targum, the enemies of Israel. Who speaks is also unclear: the man, the woman, the brothers or the daughters. Foxes were bold vineyard thieves (Nehemiah 4:3; Lamentations 5:18).
r: Nehemiah 4:3; Lamentations 5:18; Judges 15:4; Song of Songs 1:6; Song of Songs 8:11–12

a: My lover belongs to me, and I belong to him
p: The formula 'my lover is mine' returns at 6:3 and 7:10, each time in a new order.
b: The line says that each belongs to the other. Compare the covenant language 'I will be your God and you will be my people' (Ezekiel 36:28; Hosea 2:23). The three forms in the Song are: here, 'my lover belongs to me and I to him'; in 6:3 the order reverses, 'I am my lover's and my lover is mine'; and in 7:10 the second half changes to 'and his desire is toward me' (see there). Scholars read the movement as a deepening: first she has him, then she is his, and finally he wants her. 'The one who grazes among the lilies' is either the man as a shepherd or a lover who feeds on her lips and breasts.
orig: דּוֹדִי לִי וַאֲנִי לוֹ (dodi li va'ani lo)
r: Song of Songs 6:3; Song of Songs 7:10; Ezekiel 36:28; Hosea 2:23

a: Until the day breathes and the shadows run away
p: 'The day breathes' means the cool breeze; it could be morning or evening, and so the verse can be a call to leave or to come.
b: The phrase yafuach hayyom returns at 4:6. 'The day breathes' recalls 'the breezy part of the day' in the garden of Eden (Genesis 3:8), which is the cool of the evening. Shadows 'flee' when the sun rises, or lengthen and merge at evening. If it is dawn, she tells him to go before the day (a night of love ends); if evening, she tells him to stay till dusk. In 4:6 the speaker sets out to the mountain of myrrh at the same time. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew image and does not choose. The same is true of the next line: sov in 'turn, my lover' can mean turn toward her or turn away, so the Plain English Translation says only 'turn'.
r: Genesis 3:8; Song of Songs 4:6

a: the mountains of Bether
p: 'Bether' may mean cleft or split mountains, be a place name, or hide a word for spices.
b: Har bether is obscure. Bether comes from a root that means 'to cut in two' (Genesis 15:10), so 'cleft mountains' or 'mountains of separation' are suggested. The Greek has 'mountains of hollows', the Latin Vulgate keeps 'Bether' as a name, and some think of a place in Judah or the Bethar of later history. In 4:6 the lover goes to 'the mountain of myrrh' and in 8:14 'the mountains of spices', and many think all three name the same place, her body as a mountain of scents. The Plain English Translation leaves 'Bether' as a name.
r: Genesis 15:10; Song of Songs 4:6; Song of Songs 8:14

a: Night after night on my bed
t: A dream or a real search?
p: The night search may be a dream, a fantasy, or an event in the poem's story.
b: Is the woman out in the dark city, or dreaming? The poem gives no sign of waking. The 'nights' are plural, as if she looked many times. Some take it as a dream or a fantasy told as a story (Murphy, Bloch), since it begins 'on my bed' and has the shape of a dream: the search, the watchmen, the sudden finding. Others take it as a scene of a young woman who breaks the rules of her house at night to find him (Exum). The second night search in 5:2–8 is darker. Whether real or imagined, it shows desire that cannot rest.
r: Song of Songs 5:2–8; Job 33:15; Hosea 2:7

a: I searched for him, but I did not find him
t: Looking for the one you love
p: The language of 'seek and not find' is used of seeking God in the prophets and in Proverbs.
b: The pair 'seek and find' (biqqesh, matsa) is the Bible's language for searching for God: 'You will look for me and you will find me, because you will search for me with all your heart' (Jeremiah 29:13) and the warning that some seek and do not find (Hosea 5:6; Proverbs 1:28). The Song reads naturally as a human search, but the vocabulary made the allegory easy. Hippolytus (about AD 200), the earliest Christian commentator on the Song, set this scene beside the women who went looking for the Lord in the dark (John 20:1, 11–18). Origen heard in it the soul's pursuit of the Word.
r: Jeremiah 29:13; Hosea 5:6; Proverbs 1:28; John 20:1; John 20:11–18

a: The watchmen found me
p: Cities had night guards who walked the walls and streets; here they are neutral, in 5:7 they strike her.
b: A walled city posted watchmen (shomerim) on the walls and in the streets at night (Psalm 127:1; Isaiah 62:6). Here they find her, she asks about her lover, and they say nothing. In 5:7 the same watchmen beat her and take her shawl, so the second search is the darker twin. The Targum and later Christian writers gave them allegorical roles (leaders of Israel; bishops or angels), but the text does not say.
r: Song of Songs 5:7; Psalm 127:1; Isaiah 62:6; Ezekiel 3:17

a: my mother's house
p: 'My mother's house' is the woman's home, where love and marriage are arranged.
b: She takes him to her mother's house and the room of the one who conceived her. The same house appears at 8:2. Rebekah ran and told 'her mother's household' what she had seen (Genesis 24:28), and Isaac brought Rebekah into 'the tent of his mother Sarah' (Genesis 24:67). Carol Meyers notes that the Song speaks of a mother's house and never a father's. The room 'of her who conceived me' also hints at the bed where she was conceived, so that her bringing him there joins his love to her own beginning.
r: Genesis 24:28; Genesis 24:67; Ruth 1:8; Song of Songs 8:2

a: do not wake love and do not stir it up / until it wants to
p: After finding him, she charges the daughters not to disturb the love she has recovered.
b: The oath of 2:7 is repeated here word for word in the Hebrew. After the search, its force changes: she has found him, brought him to her mother's room and held him, and now she asks that no one break in. The reading 'do not hurry love' fits 2:7 better; 'do not disturb' fits here. The Plain English Translation gives the same English line in all three places (2:7; 3:5; 8:4), as the Hebrew does; the differences are noted at 8:4.
r: Song of Songs 2:7; Song of Songs 8:4

a: Who is this coming up out of the wilderness
p: The 'this' is feminine in Hebrew; it may be the bride, the litter, or Israel; in Catholic liturgy, Mary.
b: The question is asked of 'this' (zot, feminine). Readings. (1) The bride, carried in the litter of 3:7 in a wedding procession. (2) The litter itself, which is feminine in Hebrew, with Solomon on it. (3) In the Targum, Israel coming up from the wilderness. (4) In the liturgy of the Catholic and Orthodox churches, Mary, and in the Assumption office the verse is sung of her rising to heaven (Latin Quae est ista quae ascendit). The same question comes at 6:10 and 8:5. 'Coming up' could mean from the dry hill country east of Jerusalem up to the city.
orig: מִי זֹאת עֹלָה מִן הַמִּדְבָּר (mi zot olah min hamidbar)
r: Song of Songs 6:10; Song of Songs 8:5; Revelation 12:1

a: with all the powders a trader sells
p: The scent comes from imported spices carried by caravans.
b: Avqat rokhel, 'powder of a trader', is a mixture of spices ground to powder, the kind a peddler (rokhel) of perfumes carried. Myrrh and frankincense came by camel from southern Arabia, along the same route as the queen of Sheba's gifts to Solomon (1 Kings 10:2, 10). The pair 'myrrh and frankincense' marks the king as rich, and the whole line describes a cloud of scent rising from the road.
r: 1 Kings 10:2; 1 Kings 10:10; Isaiah 60:6

a: Sixty warriors
p: Sixty guards stand round the king's bed; the number may echo David's mighty men.
b: Sixty is a round number that suggests a large royal guard. David had thirty heroes and a bodyguard of Cherethites and Pelethites (2 Samuel 23:23–24), and the Song counts sixty queens at 6:8. The word 'warriors' is gibborim in both places in the Masoretic text. The scroll 4QCant-a writes the first one with a waw (gibborim in full), a difference of spelling only. The bed stands for the king's safety and the wedding night, with its need of protection (see 3:8).
r: 2 Samuel 23:8; 2 Samuel 23:23; Song of Songs 6:8

a: against the dread of the nights
p: The guards stand against fear at night: of robbers, of enemies, or of the dangers of a wedding night.
b: Pachad ballelot is 'the fear in the nights', as in Psalm 91:5, the terror of night. The common view is that the guards are there against ordinary night attack. Some scholars (for example Pope) think the fear is the dread of demons that threatened a bridal chamber in popular belief; the book of Tobit tells of the demon who killed the first husbands of Sarah (Tobit 3:7–8). The text has no demons, and this is a possible echo and not a proved one.
r: Psalm 91:5; Tobit 3:7–8; Tobit 6:13–17; Proverbs 3:25

a: a litter
p: 'Apiryon', the word for Solomon's carriage, is not an ordinary Hebrew word and is used to date the Song.
b: Apiryon occurs only here. It looks like a loan word: Greek phoreion ('a litter, a thing carried') or a Persian or Sanskrit word for a couch or palanquin. If it is Greek, the verse was written after Greek words entered Hebrew (after about 330 BC); if it is Persian or Indian, it could be earlier. Most scholars who argue for a late Song also point to the she- relative (instead of asher) and pardes 'orchard' (4:13), and those who defend an early date answer that such words could be old or dialect words. The Plain English Translation says 'litter', a bed carried on poles.
r: Song of Songs 3:7; Song of Songs 4:13; Esther 1:6

a: Its inside is fitted out with love / by the daughters of Jerusalem
t: Inlaid with love, or with leather?
p: The Hebrew 'ratsuf ahavah' is unclear: 'inlaid with love', 'paved with stone', or 'with leather'.
b: Ratsuf is 'fitted, paved, inlaid' (the root is used of hot coals, ritspah, a 'pavement' in Esther 1:6). Ahavah is 'love'. Views. (1) Inlaid with love: the inside was made by the daughters as a gift of love. (2) Inlaid with a stone or leather called ahavah; a word from Arabic is proposed for 'leather', and the Greek has 'paved with stone' and then 'love from the daughters of Jerusalem' (Swete). (3) 'Fitted out lovingly', love as the manner. All three fit the sense: the litter is rich, and its inside owes something to the daughters' affection. The Plain English Translation keeps 'fitted out with love'.
orig: רָצוּף אַהֲבָה מִבְּנוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִַם (ratsuf ahavah mibbenot Yerushalayim)
r: Esther 1:6; Isaiah 6:6; Song of Songs 3:11

a: on his wedding day
p: Solomon's wedding, a general royal wedding, or in the rabbis the day God gave the Law.
b: The 'day of his wedding' is Solomon's. The mother who crowned him would be Bathsheba (compare 1 Kings 1:11–31), though no source says she crowned him at a wedding. Another view takes the scene as a typical royal or village wedding, where the groom wore a crown (Isaiah 61:10). Mishnah Taanit 4:8 reads 'the day of his wedding' as the day the Law was given at Sinai and 'the day of the gladness of his heart' as the building of the Temple. Christian readers saw Christ crowned by his mother Israel or the Church, with the crown of thorns. First Kings 3:1 says Solomon married Pharaoh's daughter early in his reign.
r: 1 Kings 1:11–31; 1 Kings 3:1; Isaiah 61:10; Ezekiel 16:12

a: Behind your veil your eyes are doves
p: 'Tsammah' is a veil, or perhaps loose locks of hair; it appears again at 4:3 and 6:7.
b: Tsammah is found in the Bible only here, at 4:3, at 6:7 and in Isaiah 47:2, where a woman is told to remove her 'veil' and bare her legs. Most take it as a thin veil. The Greek has 'your silence' (siōpēsis), probably a different way of dividing the word, and a few scholars suggest 'locks of hair'. A bride in the ancient Near East was veiled at her wedding (Genesis 24:65; 29:23), so a veil suits the setting. The doves' eyes are seen through it.
r: Isaiah 47:2; Genesis 24:65; Song of Songs 4:3; Song of Songs 6:7

a: Your hair is like a flock of goats / streaming down Mount Gilead
p: A flock of goats on a hillside is a picture of dark hair rippling, not of its shape.
b: This is the first of the four wasf poems (Arabic for 'description') in the Song: 4:1–7, 5:10–16 (her praise of him), 6:4–10 (a shorter one that repeats part of the first) and 7:1–9. A wasf praises the body part by part, here from the head down. The comparisons do not draw a face. They tell how each part strikes the lover: black goats flowing down the slope of Gilead are the shimmer of her hair as she moves; white sheep fresh from washing are teeth. Fox and Keel point out that the comparisons are about movement, color and feeling, and that the Egyptian songs and later Syrian wedding songs praise the bride the same way (Wetzstein). A reader who tries to picture a flock on a head will be puzzled, which is why the notes explain the sense.
r: Song of Songs 5:10–16; Song of Songs 6:4–10; Song of Songs 7:1–9; Jeremiah 22:6

a: The side of your face behind your veil / is like a slice of pomegranate
p: 'Raqqah' is the side of the head between eye and ear; the picture is a flush of red.
b: Raqqah is the part of the head beside the eye, a temple. Jael drove a peg through Sisera's raqqah (Judges 4:21). English versions read 'cheek' or 'temple'. The picture is of a pomegranate cut in half, red and speckled with seeds, so the face behind the veil is flushed with color. The pomegranate was a symbol of love and fertility, and the Song uses it six times in all: 4:3, 13; 6:7, 11; 7:12; 8:2.
r: Judges 4:21; Song of Songs 4:13; Song of Songs 6:7; Song of Songs 6:11

a: Your neck is like David's tower
p: 'The tower of David' is an unknown tower hung with shields, a picture of a neck decked with ornaments.
b: No ancient source names a 'tower of David' before this verse, and the one later called by that name in Jerusalem is Herod's citadel. The picture is of a high, straight tower hung with a thousand shields. The word for 'tiers' (talpiyyot) is obscure and appears only here. Some derive it from words for 'rows' or 'hill of mouths'. Shields were hung on a wall to show strength (1 Kings 10:16–17; Ezekiel 27:10–11). The comparison is probably about a long neck, upright and strung with gold chains.
r: 1 Kings 10:16–17; Ezekiel 27:10–11; Nehemiah 3:25

a: Your breasts, both of them, are like two fawns
p: The Song speaks of breasts with the plain Hebrew word 'shadayim' and with tender images.
b: Shadayim is the ordinary word for breasts (Genesis 49:25; Ezekiel 16:7). The Song uses it in 1:13, 4:5, 7:3, 7:7–8, 8:1, 8:8 and 8:10. It does not use a hint or a euphemism, and this Plain English Translation does not either. The picture of twin fawns grazing among the lilies stresses softness, shyness and play. Many take the lilies for the lily-covered ground or the lips and flesh themselves (see 5:13). Proverbs 5:19, where the husband is told to be satisfied with his wife's breasts at all times, uses a different word, dadeha (see the variant at 1:2).
orig: שְׁנֵי שָׁדַיִךְ כִּשְׁנֵי עֳפָרִים תְּאוֹמֵי צְבִיָּה
r: Proverbs 5:19; Genesis 49:25; Ezekiel 16:7; Song of Songs 7:3

a: the mountain of myrrh
p: The mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense may be her body, or the Temple, or Calvary.
b: The speaker says he will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense as the day breathes (the same line as 2:17). Most modern readers take the mountain as her body, a place of scent, as in 'the mountain of spices' (8:14). Jewish tradition took it as Mount Moriah and the Temple, where incense burned (Genesis 22:2; 2 Chronicles 3:1). Christian writers took it as Calvary, where Christ was anointed for burial with myrrh (John 19:39). Both readings find the Song's spices in a holy place.
r: Song of Songs 2:17; Song of Songs 8:14; Genesis 22:2; 2 Chronicles 3:1; John 19:39

a: and you have no blemish
p: 'Tota pulchra es' in the Latin Bible became a Marian text; the Hebrew says a woman has no blemish.
b: Mum is 'blemish' or 'defect', the word for a flaw that disqualified an animal for sacrifice or a priest for service (Leviticus 21:17–23; 22:20). The Latin of the Vulgate reads Tota pulchra es, amica mea, et macula non est in te ('You are altogether beautiful, my friend, and there is no stain in you'), and these words are used in the Catholic liturgy for Mary, notably on the feast of the Immaculate Conception. Protestant churches do not apply the verse to Mary. Ephesians 5:27 speaks of the church 'without spot or blemish', an echo and not a quotation of the Song.
r: Leviticus 21:17–23; Ephesians 5:27; Song of Songs 6:9; Song of Songs 6:10; Revelation 12:1

a: from the top of Amana, / from the top of Senir and Hermon
p: The woman is called from the high northern mountains, lion country, down to the lover.
b: Lebanon is the long mountain range north of Israel, famous for cedar. Hermon is its southern peak (over 9,000 feet), and Senir is the Amorite name for Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9; 1 Chronicles 5:23). Amana is another peak or a river near Damascus (compare the river Abana, 2 Kings 5:12). The lions' dens and leopards' hills make it a wild, remote place. She seems to be far away or unreachable; his call to come down is a call to come near. The Hebrew tashuri can mean 'come down', 'look' or 'journey'. The Greek takes Amana as 'faith' (apo archēs pisteōs, 'from the start of faith').
r: Deuteronomy 3:9; 1 Chronicles 5:23; 2 Kings 5:12; Ezekiel 27:5

a: my sister, my bride
p: 'Sister' is a lovers' word, as in Egyptian love songs; it is not a blood tie.
b: Achoti kallah. In 4:8 she is first called 'bride'; here, in 4:9, she is also 'my sister' for the first time. 'Sister' as a pet name for a lover is very common in Egyptian love songs, where the man says 'my sister' and the woman says 'my brother', and nobody means a blood relative (Fox). The use is easy to misread, as Abraham's 'she is my sister' (Genesis 12:13; 20:2) and the incest laws (Leviticus 18:9) have a different sense. The word 'sister' adds to 'bride' the sense of equal, close and familiar. In 8:8 the speakers call her 'our sister', and there it is a family relation.
r: Genesis 12:13; Leviticus 18:9; Song of Songs 5:1; Song of Songs 8:8

a: with just one of your eyes
p: The Hebrew says 'with one of your eyes', which most read as one glance; the Qere changes 'one' from masculine to feminine.
b: The text reads literally 'with one from your eyes', and the second half has 'with one chain from your necklaces' (anaq is a necklace or pendant). The Ketiv writes 'one' as masculine (be'echad) and the Qere reads it as feminine (be'achat), which suits 'eye', a feminine noun. The meaning of 'one of your eyes' is a single look, the lightning of a glance. A few readers think it is a deliberately odd word picture: he is struck by an eye alone, as by a single jewel.
r: Song of Songs 4:10; Proverbs 6:25

a: Under your tongue are honey and milk
t: Honey and milk under the tongue
p: 'Honey and milk' is the Bible's picture of the promised land; the same honey drips from the foreign woman's lips in Proverbs.
b: 'A land flowing with milk and honey' is the Bible's phrase for the promised land (Exodus 3:8). Here the two are under her tongue, as if the kiss were the land itself. The Hebrew 'honey from the comb' (nofet) drips from her lips, and the same words describe the lips of the 'strange woman' in Proverbs 5:3, which become bitter in the end (Proverbs 5:4). The Song uses the image in a good sense, and Proverbs warns against its misuse, so the two books show opposite sides of one image.
r: Exodus 3:8; Proverbs 5:3; Proverbs 5:4; Proverbs 16:24; Psalm 19:10

a: a garden with a lock on it
p: The garden is the woman, closed to all but him; the image echoes Eden and the cistern of Proverbs.
b: A garden is a walled place where things grow, and a spring is the source of life. Together with the 'sealed' fountain they picture a woman who is reserved for one man. Compare Proverbs 5:15–18, where the husband is told to drink from his own cistern and let his fountain be blessed, and Genesis 2:8–15, where the first garden had a spring that watered it. Latin tradition called Mary the hortus conclusus ('enclosed garden') and fons signatus ('sealed fountain'). The Plain English Translation's 'garden with a lock on it' says only that she is closed until she herself opens (4:16). The next verses show a garden full of fruit, not an empty one.
r: Proverbs 5:15–18; Genesis 2:8–15; Song of Songs 4:16; Song of Songs 5:1

a: What grows from you is an orchard
p: 'Pardes' is a Persian word for a walled park; it is part of the evidence for the Song's date.
b: Pardes comes from an old Persian word (pairidaeza, 'walled enclosure') and gave English 'paradise'. It occurs in the Bible only here, in Ecclesiastes 2:5 and in Nehemiah 2:8, all after the Persian conquest, or in books that may be. Defenders of an early date say a Persian word could have reached Israel earlier. Shelachayikh ('your shoots') is also unclear: it is 'your growths', or 'your water channels' (from a root meaning 'to send'), or a euphemism for the woman's body. The Plain English Translation says 'what grows from you'.
r: Ecclesiastes 2:5; Nehemiah 2:8; Song of Songs 4:12

a: calamus and cinnamon
p: The imported spices (not henna) could not be grown in Israel; the garden is poetry, not botany.
b: The list names henna, nard, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, frankincense, myrrh and aloes. Henna grew in Israel (1:14), but nard came from the Himalayas, cinnamon from Sri Lanka or South Asia, aloes (a fragrant wood, not the skin plant) from Southeast Asia, frankincense and myrrh from Arabia. They arrived by caravan and ship, many by way of Sheba (1 Kings 10:10). Some, like cinnamon and calamus, were also in the sacred anointing oil (Exodus 30:23). A garden with all of these is a dream of Solomon's wealth, which the woman's body is made to resemble. Proverbs 7:17 lists myrrh, aloes and cinnamon for the foreign woman's bed.
r: Exodus 30:23; 1 Kings 10:10; Proverbs 7:17; Psalm 45:8

a: a well of living water
p: 'Living water' is running water; the phrase is also used of God and, in John 4, of Jesus' gift.
b: Mayim chayyim is fresh, flowing water, as opposed to the still water of a cistern. In Jeremiah 2:13 God is called the 'fountain of living water', which his people abandoned. In John 4:10–14 Jesus offers the Samaritan woman 'living water' at a well. The Song is not quoted there, but the pair of garden and well may stand behind the Christian reading of Song 4:15 as the Spirit or the grace given to the Church. In the Song itself the woman is both the garden and the spring that feeds the gardens.
r: Jeremiah 2:13; John 4:10–14; Proverbs 5:15–16; Zechariah 14:8

a: Wake up, north wind!
p: The cold north wind and the warm south wind are called to stir the garden; the verb for 'wake up' is the one in the oath.
b: The north wind is cold and clear and the south wind warm and humid; together they set the scents flowing. The verb 'wake up' (uri) is the same root as in the oath, 'do not wake love' (2:7; 3:5; 8:4). The woman now calls to the winds to wake the garden, using the verb of the oath. In Swete's Greek the next line, 'let my lover come down to his garden', begins his verse 5:1. The scents 'flow' (yizzelu) like water, as the spring does in 4:15.
r: Song of Songs 2:7; Song of Songs 3:5; Song of Songs 8:4; Genesis 3:8

a: Let my lover come into his garden
p: She, not he, opens the garden: 'my garden' becomes 'his garden' by her invitation.
b: The woman speaks of the garden first as 'my garden' and then, in the same breath, as 'his garden'. The unlocking (the garden was locked and sealed in 4:12) is her act, in her words. Trible and Exum find in this a woman who owns her sexuality and gives it; the man's own words, 'I have come into my garden' (5:1), answer her. Some readers see the exchange as a model of consent in marriage. Others warn against reading modern ideas of consent into an ancient poem. Whatever the answer, the Song makes no one but the woman the one who invites.
r: Song of Songs 4:12; Song of Songs 5:1; Genesis 2:15; Genesis 3:23

a: I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride
p: He answers her invitation: he comes, gathers, eats and drinks; every verb is a delight of the garden.
b: The man answers 4:16 with five verbs: he has come, gathered, eaten, drunk and (next line) invited friends to eat and drink. 'My garden' now belongs to him in her gift. The honeycomb, honey, wine and milk are the foods of the promised land (Exodus 3:8) and of the lovers' own pleasure; in Proverbs 5:15–19 the same drinking is told to a husband. The scene is also an Eden, a garden entered, enjoyed and not forbidden. Rabbinic readers take the verse as God accepting Israel's offerings, and Christian readers as Christ receiving the gifts of the Church.
r: Song of Songs 4:12; Song of Songs 4:16; Proverbs 5:15–19; Genesis 2:8–17

a: Eat, friends! Drink
p: The unnamed voice of 5:1c may be the man, the woman, the chorus, or God.
b: Nothing in the Hebrew says who calls the friends (re'im) to eat and drink. Views. (1) The man, inviting guests to the wedding feast he has made. (2) The chorus (the friends or the daughters), blessing the couple at the end of a wedding. (3) The woman. (4) God, blessing a union he has made; this is the old Jewish and Christian reading, where the divine voice approves the love of Israel or the Church. Because the chapter shifts voice at 5:2 without notice, the speaker of 5:1c is a joint in the book's structure. Many scholars see it as the end of the wedding section (3:6–5:1).
r: Song of Songs 3:6–11; Song of Songs 5:2; Proverbs 9:5

a: I was asleep, but my heart was awake
p: The line puts the whole scene at the edge of sleep; rabbis and Christian writers heard a spiritual vigilance.
b: The heart (lev) in the Bible is the mind and will as well as the feelings; 'my heart was awake' means she was alert, or half awake, or dreaming. Is what follows a dream? Many scholars say yes: the knock, the vanishing man, the beating, and the sudden question to the daughters, all have the quality of a dream (Murphy, Bloch). Song of Songs Rabbah 5:2 reads the line as Israel asleep in exile or neglecting the commandments while her heart is awake in the good deeds she still does. Christian writers read it as the soul at rest but alert to Christ's call.
r: Song of Songs 3:1; Proverbs 6:9; Genesis 28:16; Revelation 3:20

a: My lover is knocking
p: The knocking lover is a Song image; Revelation 3:20 may echo it, but does not quote it.
b: In Revelation 3:20 the risen Christ stands at the door and knocks, and if anyone opens he will come in and eat with that person. The picture of a lover at the door who is slow to be admitted has led Christian readers to hear an echo of the Song, and Origen read 5:2 so. The Greek of Song 5:2 and of Revelation 3:20 both use the verb krouō, 'knock', which strengthens the echo. It is still an echo and not a quotation: Revelation does not cite the Song, and its words are a letter to Laodicea. Song of Songs Rabbah 5:2 has God ask Israel to open to him a space as small as the eye of a needle, and promises to open one wide as a hall. In the poem the lover simply knocks; the woman holds back, which sets the second night search going.
r: Revelation 3:20; Luke 12:36; Song of Songs 5:5–6

a: my dove, my perfect one
p: 'Tammati' means whole or complete: flawless, but also in one piece and sincere.
b: Tammati comes from tam, 'whole, complete, innocent', the word for Job's integrity (Job 1:1) and for the faultless life of Psalm 15:2. It sums up the 'no blemish' of 4:7 and returns at 6:9. It is not a claim of sinlessness but a love-name for a woman who is undivided, all there. The strings of names (sister, darling, dove, perfect one) pile up like the endearments of the Egyptian songs.
r: Job 1:1; Psalm 15:2; Song of Songs 6:9; Song of Songs 4:7

a: I have taken off my tunic: how could I put it on again?
p: Her reply to his knock has been read as laziness, teasing, or the first step of an old 'hard to get' game.
b: The woman's answer is that she has already undressed and washed her feet. Some call it a polite excuse, some a tease, since the Song's lovers play at hiding and finding (2:9, 14). Others point out that 'feet' can be a delicate word for the body (Ruth 3:4, 7; Isaiah 7:20), so that both lines hint at what she is not wearing and may still do. Allegorical writers heard a soul that has put on the comfort of the world and does not want to move (Origen; Gregory the Great). Whatever the tone, the next verse shows her desire coming back to her.
r: Ruth 3:4; Ruth 3:7; Isaiah 7:20; Exodus 4:25

a: sent his hand in through the opening
p: The Hebrew 'yad' (hand) and 'chor' (hole) are plain words that can both mean more than they say.
b: Chor is a hole, as in a door where the latch-cord or bolt could be reached from outside (a hole in a wall or the hole of a snake, Isaiah 11:8). Yad is 'hand', and in the Bible it can also stand for the male organ (Isaiah 57:8, 10 in a hard passage). Many scholars hear the verse on both levels: the lover reaches through a door's opening, and the same lines speak of love-making. The Plain English Translation translates the plain words and leaves the double sense to the reader and the note. 'Sent' means he reached out his hand, not that he threw it.
r: Isaiah 57:8; Isaiah 11:8; Song of Songs 5:5

a: my insides churned for him
p: 'Me'ay' means the inner organs: belly, womb or bowels; they are the seat of deep feeling.
b: Me'im (inner parts) is the Hebrew for the gut, the womb, the place where deep feeling is felt. It is used for the stirring of tenderness (Jeremiah 31:20, 'my insides churn for him') and for dread (Jeremiah 4:19; Isaiah 16:11). 'Churned' is the verb hamu, 'roar, murmur', as of the sea or a crowd (Psalm 46:3). The same verb is used of God's insides stirring for Ephraim. The Greek has 'my belly was troubled'. The same Hebrew word (me'im) is behind 5:14, where the Plain English Translation says 'belly' for the man (see the gloss there).
r: Jeremiah 31:20; Jeremiah 4:19; Isaiah 16:11; Song of Songs 5:14

a: myrrh dripped from my hands
p: Myrrh runs from her fingers onto the door handles: she has perfumed herself, or he left it there.
b: Why does myrrh drip from her hands? Views. (1) She had put myrrh on her hands to be ready for him. (2) He left the perfume on the bolt and she picks it up (the Hebrew 'on the handles of the bolt' can read either way). (3) It is a picture of her desire: she is flooded with the scent. The word is mor over, 'liquid myrrh', the free-flowing oil also named in Exodus 30:23. In 5:13 his lips drip the same myrrh. The Targum reads it as Israel at the Tabernacle, and Christian writers as the good works of the soul.
r: Exodus 30:23; Song of Songs 5:13; Song of Songs 1:13

a: My life went out of me when he spoke
p: 'Nefesh yatse'ah' means her life, or her whole self, went out at his voice; it can be a swoon or a rush after him.
b: Compare Genesis 35:18, where Rachel's nefesh 'went out' as she died. Here the line most likely means she faints at his voice, or her whole being rushes out to him, or she is shaken to the point of death. Some take bedabbero as 'at his word' (so the Greek), and the Plain English Translation's 'when he spoke' fits both. The line turns on the Hebrew nefesh, which the Plain English Translation translates 'my life' here and 'my whole self' when it is the one who loves.
r: Genesis 35:18; Song of Songs 1:7; Song of Songs 3:1

a: They hit me and bruised me
p: The same watchmen who were kind in 3:3 beat her; the poem says why only by silence.
b: In the first search the watchmen found her and said nothing (3:3). In the second they strike and wound her and take her shawl. Views. (1) A dream sequence, in which the search turns into a nightmare. (2) A real danger: a woman alone at night in the street could be taken for a prostitute or a thief. (3) A picture of the city's moral police, which the Song uses to show how love goes outside the rules. The Plain English Translation's 'hit' and 'bruised' are plain words. Feminist readers such as Exum note that the poem shows violence against a woman and does not blame her for it. The allegories made the watchmen into false teachers or persecutors.
r: Song of Songs 3:3; Isaiah 62:6; Hosea 2:7

a: my shawl
p: 'Radid' is a wrap worn over the clothes; Isaiah 3:23 lists it among a lady's finery.
b: Radid is a large wrap or shawl, here carried off by the guards. It is used again only in Isaiah 3:23, in a list of women's finery that the Lord will take away, and in Genesis 24:65 Rebekah's veil is another word (tsa'if). Some English versions say 'veil' or 'cloak'. For a woman to lose it in public was to be stripped of her protection and her modesty. The Plain English Translation keeps 'veil' for tsammah (4:1, 3; 6:7) and 'shawl' for this word.
r: Isaiah 3:23; Genesis 24:65; Genesis 38:14

a: I make you swear, daughters of Jerusalem: / if you find my lover, what will you tell him?
p: This oath does not ask the daughters to leave love alone; it asks them to carry a message.
b: The charge to the daughters changes form. In 2:7, 3:5 and 8:4 she forbids them to wake love; here she asks them to find her lover and tell him she is sick with love. They have now become her helpers. This is one reason some scholars treat the three 'wake not' oaths as a refrain of its own and this one as part of the second search. The daughters answer at once with the long question that begins the next section (5:9).
r: Song of Songs 2:7; Song of Songs 5:9; Song of Songs 6:1

a: bright and ruddy
p: 'Tsach' is clear or shining; 'adom' is red, the color of healthy skin or of David.
b: Tsach is 'clear, dazzling' (Isaiah 18:4, 'the glare of heat in the light'), so a bright, clean look; adom is 'red, ruddy', the word used of the young David (1 Samuel 16:12) and of the princes of Lamentations 4:7, whose bodies were 'redder than coral'. So he is a vigorous young man with a healthy flush. The next word, dagul, is 'marked out' or 'banner-like', from the same root as 'banner' (2:4; 6:4).
r: 1 Samuel 16:12; Lamentations 4:7; Song of Songs 2:4

a: His head is gold, the finest gold
p: The man's praise is built from gold, ivory, marble and sapphire, the stuff of a statue.
b: The description of the man (5:10–16) runs from head to legs in costly materials: gold, ivory, lapis, marble and gold bases. Marvin Pope suggested that it echoes the descriptions of cult statues in the ancient Near East; one thinks too of the image with a head of gold in Daniel 2:32. The man is praised as if he were a work of the finest craft, as the woman is praised as a tower or garden. Egyptian and Sumerian praise of the king or a god used similar images. The effect is that he is not heavy or cold, but that he is gleaming, strong and rare.
r: Daniel 2:32; Song of Songs 5:14–15; Song of Songs 7:1

a: sitting beside the full water
p: 'Al milet' is unclear: beside a brimming pool, or set in a setting like a jewel.
b: Mil'et is 'fullness' (the plural millu'im names the settings of stones in the high priest's breastplate, Exodus 25:7; 28:17). So the doves sit by 'full' (brimming) water, or the eyes are set in their sockets as jewels in their settings. Both the Plain English Translation and the old Greek take the first, the Greek having 'sitting on fullnesses'. The picture is of dark eyes, with white around them (milk), set within a face as doves sit on a pool.
r: Exodus 25:7; Exodus 28:17; Song of Songs 5:12

a: stones from Tarshish
p: 'Tarshish' names a far western place; the stone is probably the golden beryl or chrysolite.
b: Tarshish stands for a far western land and port, probably Tartessos in Spain, whose ships carried metal (Jeremiah 10:9; Ezekiel 27:12). The 'stone of Tarshish' is named in the high priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:20) and in Ezekiel 1:16 and Daniel 10:6; it is often thought to be golden beryl or chrysolite. The 'rods of gold' are round cylinders or rings. So his hands are gold set with jewels, an image of strong, ringed fingers.
r: Exodus 28:20; Ezekiel 1:16; Daniel 10:6; Jeremiah 10:9

a: His belly is a plate of ivory / covered with sapphires
p: 'Me'im' is the belly or inner part; 'sappir' is lapis lazuli (a deep blue stone), not our sapphire.
b: The Hebrew me'av is the same noun as 'my insides' (me'ay) in 5:4, so a reader of the Hebrew hears the one word twice and may mean the belly, the loins or the whole trunk. It is not beten, the word used for her belly in 7:2. The 'plate of ivory' (esheth shen) is a smooth, creamy surface, and the 'sapphires' (sappirim) are lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone set in gold (Exodus 24:10). Many read the veins showing blue under skin. Others think of a throne of ivory overlaid with gold (1 Kings 10:18).
r: Exodus 24:10; 1 Kings 10:18; Song of Songs 5:4; Song of Songs 7:2

a: This one is my lover, and this one is my friend
p: 'Re'i' (my friend) is the man's only title of friendship; the woman is his 're'ayah'.
b: The woman ends her praise with two words for him: dodi ('my lover') and re'i ('my friend'). In the Song the man calls her ra'yati ('my darling', literally 'my friend') nine times. This is the only time she calls him re'i, so the pair is complete: each is lover and friend. Compare the proverb that a friend (re'a) loves at all times (Proverbs 17:17). Love in the Song is erotic and also companionable.
orig: זֶה דוֹדִי וְזֶה רֵעִי (zeh dodi vezeh re'i)
r: Proverbs 17:17; Song of Songs 1:9; Song of Songs 2:2

a: My lover has gone down to his garden
p: She answers the daughters at once: he is in his garden. The garden is her body, or a real place, or the Church.
b: The daughters ask where he has gone (6:1) and she knows. She who ran through the city a moment ago now says he has gone 'to his garden', to the beds of spice. Views. (1) The garden is her: he has gone down to her, and she is not lost; her search ends in the same place as her longing. (2) It is a real garden, and he is a shepherd-gardener there (compare 2:16; 1:7). (3) It is the Church, where Christ feeds his flock and gathers lilies (Origen, Gregory of Nyssa), or the Temple, where God is present (the rabbis). In 5:1 he came to 'my garden', so the move from 'my' to 'his' garden keeps the two together.
r: Song of Songs 4:16; Song of Songs 5:1; Song of Songs 2:16

a: like Tirzah
p: Tirzah was the capital of the northern kingdom before Samaria; its name sounds like 'pleasing'.
b: Tirzah was a northern city, the capital of Israel under Jeroboam and his successors until Omri moved the capital to Samaria (1 Kings 14:17; 15:21, 33; 16:8–24). Its name is close to the Hebrew ratsah, 'to be pleasing'. To set 'Tirzah' beside 'Jerusalem' is to name the two chief cities of north and south together, and since Tirzah lost its rank after about 880 BC, some scholars use this as a sign of an early date or a northern writer. Others say a later poet could name an old city for its beauty. Others take the pair as a pun: 'beautiful as pleasing, lovely as the city of peace'.
r: 1 Kings 14:17; 1 Kings 15:21; 1 Kings 16:8–24; Joshua 12:24

a: fearsome as troops with banners
p: 'Ayumah' means awe-inspiring; 'nidgalot' occurs only here and in 6:10.
b: Ayumah is 'terrible, awe-inspiring', the sort of look that makes a man stand still (Habakkuk 1:7 uses it of the Chaldeans). Nidgalot is a rare form from degel, 'banner': 'bannered ones', 'troops with banners', or, in the Greek, 'drawn up in ranks'. The Latin Vulgate has castrorum acies ordinata, 'an army set in order'. The Song means that her glance has the force of a marching army, which is why in 6:5 he asks her to turn her eyes away. Some propose that nidgalot means 'stars in order', following 6:10.
r: Habakkuk 1:7; Song of Songs 2:4; Song of Songs 6:10

a: for they overpower me
p: 'Hirhivuni' is rare and means 'they make me proud', 'bold' or 'stir me up'; the sense is that her eyes are too much for him.
b: The verb hirhiv usually means 'to make wide' or 'to be bold' (Psalm 138:3, 'you put boldness in me'; Proverbs 6:3, 'badger your neighbor'). The versions differ: 'they have overcome me' (King James Version) and the Greek 'they gave me wings'. The sense is that her gaze undoes him, or gives him a rush he cannot hold. The Plain English Translation says 'overpower' and leaves the cause: her eyes are too strong for him.
r: Psalm 138:3; Proverbs 6:3; Song of Songs 4:9

a: Your teeth are like a flock of ewes / coming up from the washing
p: Lines from 4:1–3 return almost word for word; the repetition may be a refrain or a sign of separate poems.
b: 6:5b–7 repeats 4:1b–3 with small changes: 'ewes' for 'shorn ewes', 'from Gilead' for 'from Mount Gilead', no doves in the eyes. Views. (1) A deliberate refrain, as in a ballad, to mark the second half of the book (Murphy, Exum). (2) The reuse of a stock set of images by different poets, which suits an anthology (Fox). (3) A sign of a long poem built around the praise of the woman, a unity read as developing (Garrett). The repetition is one of the strongest arguments in the debate about whether the Song is one poem or many.
r: Song of Songs 4:1–3; Song of Songs 7:1–9

a: Sixty are the queens and eighty the concubines
p: The numbers are a ladder: sixty, eighty, then too many to count; they are smaller than Solomon's 1,000.
b: A king's wives and concubines show his wealth. First Kings 11:3 says Solomon had 700 wives who were princesses and 300 concubines, and warns that they turned his heart away. The Song's sixty and eighty are far fewer, so the numbers are not Solomon's. They rise in steps (60, 80, countless), a form of numerical saying (as in Proverbs 30:15–31), to set up the point: against any number of women, one is the lover's one. Ecclesiastes 7:28 and 2:8 give the preacher's mixed view of the same court.
r: 1 Kings 11:1–3; Ecclesiastes 2:8; Ecclesiastes 7:28; Proverbs 30:15–31

a: One is my dove, my perfect one
t: 'One': the Church, Israel, or the only one
p: The word 'one' is read as Israel's oneness, the Church's unity, or simply the lover's single choice.
b: The man has many to choose from (6:8), and says there is one for him. In Jewish reading she is Israel, the one nation of God in a world of many (compare Deuteronomy 6:4, 'the LORD is one'). In Christian reading she is the Church, one among many sects: Cyprian (about AD 251) quotes this verse in his treatise On the Unity of the Catholic Church to say that the Church has only one mother, and Pope Boniface VIII's bull Unam Sanctam (1302) uses it too. (In the Latin Bible, which Cyprian and Boniface used, the verse is numbered 6:8.) In the plain reading, the Song stands apart from a world of royal harems by naming one beloved. The word for 'pure' (barah) is the favorite or the chosen.
r: Deuteronomy 6:4; Song of Songs 2:10; Song of Songs 5:2; Ephesians 4:4–6

a: Who is this looking down like the dawn
p: The three lights echo praise of the goddess Inanna or Ishtar in Mesopotamian songs, without any worship in the Song.
b: The woman is compared to dawn, moon and sun, then to the armies of 6:4. Othmar Keel and others point out that Mesopotamian songs praise Inanna or Ishtar as the morning star and as a terror in war, and that Ugarit had a god named Shachar, 'Dawn'. The Song borrows the grand language without any worship of a goddess; it is a poetic way to say that the woman shines. Catholic liturgy, with the Latin pulchra ut luna, electa ut sol, uses the verse for Mary (see 4:7). Whether the group who spoke 6:9 (queens and concubines) speak this too is argued; see the card.
r: Song of Songs 6:4; Isaiah 14:12; Job 3:9; Revelation 12:1

a: My longing set me / among the chariots of my noble people
p: Nearly every word of this verse is disputed; it may name 'Amminadib', or say 'my noble people'.
b: Hebrew: lo yada'ti nafshi samatni markevot 'ammi nadiv. Views. (1) 'Before I knew it, my desire put me in the chariots of my noble people', a sudden swing into a royal procession or a sudden rush of love. (2) 'Ammi-nadib' is a name, like the Aminadab of Exodus 6:23, and she is carried among his chariots; the Greek and Latin read the name (see the variant). (3) The words are 'my people, a prince', a pet name for her lover. (4) A damaged text, which several scholars repair. The Plain English Translation keeps to the Hebrew and does not choose.
orig: לֹא יָדַעְתִּי נַפְשִׁי שָׂמַתְנִי מַרְכְּבוֹת עַמִּי נָדִיב
r: Exodus 6:23; Numbers 1:7; Ruth 4:19–20; Song of Songs 6:13

a: Come back, come back, Shulammite!
p: The Shulammite is probably 'the woman from Shunem'; Shelomoh (Solomon) and Abishag have been proposed.
b: Hashulammit occurs only here. Views. (1) A woman of Shunem (Shunem is a town in Issachar; Joshua 19:18), with l and n exchanged; the Greek has Soumaneitis, 'Shunammite', and the Latin Sulamitis. Abishag from Shunem warmed old King David (1 Kings 1:3) and a rich woman of Shunem gave Elisha a room (2 Kings 4:8). (2) The feminine of 'Solomon' (Shelomoh), so 'Solomon's woman', or a pet name from shalom (peace). (3) A woman of a place called Shulam. Some older readers made her the speaker of the whole Song, and then Abishag its heroine; that is a view, not a fact.
r: 1 Kings 1:3; 2 Kings 4:8; Joshua 19:18; 1 Samuel 28:4

a: Why do you look at the Shulammite / as at the dance of the two camps?
t: Hebrew verse numbering and the dance
p: In the Hebrew Bible this verse is 7:1; in the Plain English Translation it is 6:13. The dance of Mahanaim is the second question.
b: The Hebrew Bible numbers this verse 7:1, so Hebrew chapter 6 has 12 verses and Hebrew chapter 7 has 14, against 13 and 13 in English (the Plain English Translation follows the English numbering, as the rest of the site does; the Hebrew number is given in the source files). Who asks the question? The chorus (they want to look) and she, or he, answers 'why do you look?'. The question is whether the Shulammite is worth the look (the crowd may think her a mere country girl) and the answer, 7:1–9, is a long wasf.
r: Song of Songs 7:1; Song of Songs 6:12

a: the dance of the two camps
p: Mahanaim, 'two camps', is the place where Jacob met angels; the dance may be a sword dance at a wedding.
b: Machanayim ('two camps') is the name Jacob gave the place in Gilead where angels met him (Genesis 32:1–2); it became a city (2 Samuel 2:8; 17:24). The 'dance of Mahanaim' may be a dance there, a dance of two lines facing each other, or a dance named after the angels' camps. Wetzstein recorded a sword dance performed by Syrian brides during the wedding week, and Delitzsch took the Shulammite to be dancing it. The Plain English Translation has 'the two camps' and leaves the name for the note.
r: Genesis 32:1–2; 2 Samuel 2:8; 2 Samuel 17:24; 1 Kings 4:14

a: How lovely your steps are in your sandals
t: The praise that starts at the feet
p: The fourth praise runs from the feet up; she is moving, perhaps dancing, and he watches.
b: This is the fourth and longest wasf (see 4:1). It runs the other way from the first, from her feet up to her hair (7:1–5), and it is about a woman in motion: her steps, the curve of her thighs, the sway of her body. The previous verse, 6:13, speaks of a dance, so she is probably dancing, and the eye of the poem rises as she turns. Her feet in sandals show she is out of doors (compare Ezekiel 16:10). The speaker is the man, or the chorus who asked to look (6:13).
r: Song of Songs 6:13; Song of Songs 4:1–7; Ezekiel 16:10

a: you daughter of a nobleman
p: 'Bat nadiv' is a title of honor: she has the rank of a noble's daughter, whatever her birth.
b: Nadiv means 'generous, noble', and a nadiv is a noble, a prince (Psalm 47:9; Proverbs 8:16). The word returns from 6:12, where it was part of the obscure 'my noble people' or 'Amminadib'. The Shulammite is a country girl whose brothers made her work in the vineyards (1:6), and here she is called a nobleman's daughter in a compliment about how she carries herself. The Greek here has thygater Nadab, 'daughter of Nadab', taking the word as a name, which matches its reading of 6:12 (see the variant there). The same love-talk calls a couple king and queen (1:4; 3:11).
r: Psalm 47:9; Proverbs 8:16; Song of Songs 6:12

a: The curves of your thighs are like jewels
p: 'Yarekh' is the thigh or the hip; elsewhere it is a gentle word for the loins.
b: Yarekh is the upper leg or the hip, and in other places it is the place from which children are said to come (Genesis 46:26, where the Hebrew 'from his thigh' is Plain English Translation 'those who sprang from his own body'; Genesis 24:2, 'Put your hand under my thigh'). The curves (chamuqim, from a verb meaning 'to turn') are the line where thigh meets hip. Chala'im (the Plain English Translation's 'jewels') is a rare word for ornaments. The 'master craftsman' is a skilled artisan (a related word, amon, is used of Wisdom beside the LORD in Proverbs 8:30, in one reading). The Plain English Translation says 'thighs' in every place, as the term list asks.
r: Genesis 24:2; Genesis 46:26; Proverbs 8:30

a: Your navel is a round bowl
p: 'Shorer' means navel (Ezekiel 16:4); some read it as a euphemism for the womb or the vulva.
b: Shorer is the navel or umbilical cord (Ezekiel 16:4). The Greek renders it omphalos, 'navel'. Pope and others propose a euphemism for the female sex organ, since the praise has just climbed through the thighs and is now at the belly, and the 'mixed wine' that never runs short fits that; others say the navel itself suffices, a cup that is always full. The 'round bowl' (aggan hassahar) is a rounded basin (sahar, 'roundness' or 'moon'). Mezeg is spiced wine mixed with water. The Plain English Translation says 'navel' and leaves the second sense to the note.
r: Ezekiel 16:4; Proverbs 9:2; Song of Songs 8:2

a: Your belly is a pile of wheat
t: Wheat, lilies and Ruth's threshing floor
p: A heap of wheat is the harvest; at the threshing floor in Ruth 3, a man lies down at the far end of a grain pile.
b: Beten is the belly or womb. A pile of winnowed wheat is golden and rounded, and the picture is of harvest plenty. Ruth 3:7 sets a night scene by the threshing floor: Boaz goes 'to lie down at the far end of the grain pile', and Ruth comes in quietly and lies at his feet. The two books share a country setting of grain, night and a man and woman, and in both the woman takes the first step. The 'lilies' around the heap are like a fence of flowers (compare the lilies of 2:16; 4:5; 6:2).
r: Ruth 3:7; Ruth 3:2; Song of Songs 2:16; Song of Songs 4:5

a: In Heshbon, by the gate of Bat-rabbim, / your eyes are pools
p: Heshbon was a Transjordanian city known for its reservoirs; her eyes are as deep and calm as pools.
b: Heshbon was the city of Sihon the Amorite king (Numbers 21:25–30), east of the Dead Sea in what became Moab and Ammon's land; the prophets name its fall (Isaiah 15:4; Jeremiah 48:2). Its 'pools' were large cisterns in the dry hill country; modern excavations at Tell Hesban found large reservoirs. Bat-rabbim ('daughter of many') is not known as a place: it may be a gate named for the crowds who came through it. The picture is of deep, still, gleaming eyes. Another place name in the same verse, Damascus, lies far to the north.
orig: עֵינַיִךְ בְּרֵכוֹת בְּחֶשְׁבּוֹן עַל שַׁעַר בַּת רַבִּים
r: Numbers 21:25–30; Isaiah 15:4; Jeremiah 48:2; Isaiah 16:8–9

a: Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon
p: A tower on the Lebanon range watching toward Damascus is a proud, straight nose.
b: The comparison sounds odd to modern ears. A tall tower on the Lebanon heights, watching toward Damascus (the capital of Aram), is an image of a straight, strong, noble nose; for the ancient world a prominent nose was a sign of dignity. The Song's images are about impression: she is proud, upright and watchful. Solomon is said to have built towers in Lebanon (1 Kings 9:19), and the tower of David in 4:4 and the ivory tower in 7:4 make a set of towers in her body. Such towers are also used in 8:10, where the woman says her breasts are towers.
orig: אַפֵּךְ כְּמִגְדַּל הַלְּבָנוֹן צוֹפֶה פְּנֵי דַמָּשֶׂק
r: 1 Kings 9:19; Song of Songs 4:4; Song of Songs 8:10; 2 Chronicles 8:6

a: Your head upon you is like Mount Carmel
p: 'Carmel' means garden-land: a green headland; her hair has a deep purple-black gleam.
b: Carmel is the mountain ridge on the Mediterranean coast; its name means 'garden land' or 'orchard', and it was known for its lush green (Isaiah 35:2; Amos 1:2). So her head rises over her shoulders as Carmel rises above the sea. Argaman is purple wool, dyed with the sea snail, the costly color of kings (Judges 8:26; Esther 8:15). So her hair has a deep, glossy sheen. Dallat rosh ('the hair of your head') might be 'the hanging threads of the loom', as in Isaiah 38:12: long strands hanging down.
orig: רֹאשֵׁךְ עָלַיִךְ כַּכַּרְמֶל וְדַלַּת רֹאשֵׁךְ כָּאַרְגָּמָן
r: Isaiah 35:2; Amos 1:2; Judges 8:26; Esther 8:15; Isaiah 38:12

a: A king is bound by its tresses
p: The king is held in her hair: her power over him, or over any king, is the Song's turn.
b: Rahatim are 'tresses', or channels or troughs (Genesis 30:38; Exodus 2:16 use it for watering troughs), so her hair falls like water in channels. The king 'bound' by it is her captive. Views. (1) The king is the lover, who is held by her. (2) The king is Solomon as a stock figure: even he is her prisoner, a theme the book returns to at 8:11–12. (3) In the allegories the King is God or Christ, bound by love for his people (Origen). In every reading the king, who rules everyone, is ruled by her.
r: Genesis 30:38; Exodus 2:16; Song of Songs 1:4; Song of Songs 8:11–12

a: love, among the delights
p: 'Ahavah' is 'love', which here seems to be a form of address; the Greek has 'love, in your delights'.
b: The Hebrew ahavah ba-ta'anugim is literally 'love, in delights'. Is 'love' a name for her ('O love', as in 'my darling'), or an abstract noun for what is happening ('what delight love has')? Some scholars read ahuvah, 'beloved woman', by a slight change. The Greek has agapē, en truphais sou, 'love, in your pleasures'. The Qumran scroll 4QCant-a, as transcribed, writes 'how pleasant' without the 'and'. The Plain English Translation says 'love' and treats it as a form of address.
r: Song of Songs 2:7; Song of Songs 8:6

a: You are as tall as a palm tree
p: A date palm is slender, tall and heavy with fruit; the climber takes hold of its clusters.
b: The date palm (tamar) is tall and straight, and its fruit grows in thick clusters. Tamar is also a woman's name (Genesis 38; 2 Samuel 13:1), and Deborah sat under a palm (Judges 4:5). The man says he will climb it and take hold of the fruit-stalks, and wishes her breasts were clusters of the vine. Egyptian love songs speak of a girl's body as a tree and of the lover who climbs or plucks. The climbing and the clusters are plain images of desire, and the Plain English Translation keeps the plain words. Many commentators note that the scene is not a conquest but a wish ('may your breasts be...').
r: Judges 4:5; Psalm 92:12; Song of Songs 7:8

a: going down smoothly for my lover
p: The man's wine comparison is taken up by the woman in the middle of the verse.
b: The sentence begins with the man ('your mouth is like the best wine') and ends with the woman's words 'for my lover' and 'gliding over the lips of sleepers'. The Hebrew says holekh ledodi, 'going to my lover', so the speaker speaks of her lover in the third person. Some scholars treat this as the woman completing his thought: it is wine for him, and so she cuts in. Others change the text to read 'for me' (the Latin has 'for my beloved to drink'). The result is a verse with two voices in one sentence, the Song's way of showing how two lovers speak in turn. Then 7:10 is all hers.
