r: Song of Songs 1:2; Song of Songs 5:1; Song of Songs 7:10

a: his desire is toward me
p: The word 'teshuqah' occurs only here, in Genesis 3:16 and in Genesis 4:7; the Song may undo the curse.
b: Teshuqah, 'desire', is used three times in the Bible. In Genesis 3:16 God tells the woman, 'your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you'. In Genesis 4:7 sin is crouching at Cain's door, and 'its desire is for you, but you must rule over it'. In the Song, the man's desire is toward the woman, with no mention of rule. Phyllis Trible argued that this line reverses the Eden curse: the woman's desire is no longer her subjection, and the man's desire is toward her. Views on Genesis 3:16 differ (a punishment, a prediction, a desire to control him), and so does the weight put on the Song's echo. The Song says it only once.
r: Genesis 3:16; Genesis 4:7; Song of Songs 2:16; Song of Songs 6:3

a: Let us spend the night in the villages
p: 'Kefarim' can be 'villages' or 'henna bushes'; both fit.
b: Kefarim is the plural of kefar, 'village', as in the Greek (en kōmais) and the Latin. The same letters are the plural of kofer, 'henna', which the Song uses at 1:14 and 4:13. Then it would be 'let us spend the night among the henna', a scented, outdoor bed. The first reading gives a rural trip; the second recalls the henna of En-gedi. The Plain English Translation says 'villages' and leaves the second sense for the note.
r: Song of Songs 1:14; Song of Songs 4:13; Song of Songs 7:12

a: There I will give you my lovemaking
p: The woman picks the time, the place and the gift; this is the Song's boldest invitation.
b: The woman invites him out of the house, to the vineyards at dawn, to see whether the vines have budded, 'there I will give you my lovemaking' (dodai). The speaker sets the time (early), the place (the vineyard) and the gift. Compare 6:11, where the visit to the nut garden had the same list (vine, pomegranates). Her brothers made her guard other vineyards in 1:6; now she takes her lover to hers. Exum and others find in this a woman who is neither passive nor a seducer who needs to hide: she is free in her speech. The Plain English Translation translates dodai as 'my lovemaking', as at 1:2.
orig: שָׁם אֶתֵּן אֶת דֹּדַי לָךְ (sham etten et dodai lakh)
r: Song of Songs 1:6; Song of Songs 6:11; Song of Songs 8:12

a: The mandrakes give off their scent
p: Mandrakes were thought to help conception; Leah and Rachel traded them for a night with Jacob.
b: Dudaim are mandrakes, a plant with a strong smell and a forked root, popularly believed to make a woman fertile or a man potent. In Genesis 30:14–16 Reuben found mandrakes in the field and Rachel, who was childless, bought them from Leah in exchange for a night with Jacob. The sound of dudaim is close to dodim ('lovemaking') and dod ('lover'), so the word may be a pun. The mandrake blooms in winter and fruits in spring, so the setting fits the season of the poem. The Plain English Translation says 'mandrakes' as in Genesis.
r: Genesis 30:14–16; Song of Songs 7:12

a: If only someone would make you my brother
t: A wish to love in the open
p: She wishes he were her brother, so she could kiss him in public without shame.
b: A woman could kiss her brother in the street without anyone sneering, but not her lover. The wish is for freedom to show love openly. 'Who nursed at my mother's breasts' makes the tie even closer: milk-siblings are siblings. The lovers call each other 'sister' and 'brother' in other places (4:9), as in Egyptian songs, so the wish is also a play on the pet name: if only the word were true in law. Some readers see an echo of Genesis 29:11, where Jacob kisses Rachel at the well in front of the shepherds. Others note that the Song's lovers keep meeting in private and that this verse says what they long for.
orig: מִי יִתֶּנְךָ כְּאָח לִי יוֹנֵק שְׁדֵי אִמִּי
r: Genesis 29:11; Song of Songs 4:9; Song of Songs 3:4

a: spiced wine
p: 'Spiced wine' and 'pomegranate juice' are drinks of the wedding table, once more in the garden of the senses.
b: Yayin haregach is wine with spices added, a luxury drink; 'asis rimmoni is the juice of pomegranates. The drinks echo the 'wine' of 1:2 and 4:10 (love is better than wine) and the pomegranates of 4:3, 13; 6:7, 11 and 7:12. The woman who said 'your love is better than wine' now says she will give him wine to drink. The drink is the gift of herself, and the offering of a feast in her mother's house is the proper return for what she wished in 8:1.
r: Song of Songs 1:2; Song of Songs 4:10; Song of Songs 7:12

a: do not wake love and do not stir it up / until it wants to
p: The last oath has no gazelles, and the first word of the condition is 'why' where the earlier oaths had 'if'.
b: The Hebrew of 8:4 differs from 2:7 and 3:5 in two small ways. It does not name 'the gazelles or the does of the field' (although Swete's Greek still has 'the powers and the forces of the field' here, as at 2:7 and 3:5), and the condition begins mah, 'why', not im, 'if'. Scholars read mah as 'why would you wake?' or as another form of the oath's negative ('you shall not wake'), as with im. The second verb is written without its vowel letter in 8:4 (te'orerru), a difference in spelling only. The Plain English Translation gives the same English line each time, as the sense is the same. With the third oath the book closes its third cycle, and what follows (8:5–7) is the end of the argument.
r: Song of Songs 2:7; Song of Songs 3:5; Song of Songs 5:8

a: Who is this climbing up from the wilderness
p: The question is asked for the third time (3:6; 6:10); now she is leaning on her lover.
b: The three questions 'Who is this?' at 3:6, 6:10 and 8:5 each mark a new stage. First the cloud of smoke from the wilderness, then the dawn that looks down, and now a woman who leans on her lover as she climbs. Mitrapeqet, 'leaning', is the only use of the word in the Bible. It looks like a picture of ease and trust after the long journey of the book. The Catholic liturgy uses the verse for Mary at the Assumption; the Targum reads it of Israel leaning on God in her return from exile.
orig: מִי זֹאת עֹלָה מִן הַמִּדְבָּר מִתְרַפֶּקֶת עַל דּוֹדָהּ
r: Song of Songs 3:6; Song of Songs 6:10

a: Under the apple tree I woke you
p: Under the apple tree someone woke someone: the Hebrew says she woke him, but the letters allow either.
b: The line is a short speech inside the question, and the speaker is not named. The Hebrew vowel marks (the pointing) make 'you' masculine, so she woke him under the apple tree where his mother conceived or bore him; the same letters would also read 'you' as feminine, so that he woke her at the tree where her mother bore her. The apple tree was his shade in 2:3. The 'waking' repeats the oath's verb (2:7): she, who forbade others to wake love, wakes him herself, or he her. Some readers hear the apple tree as the place of conception, so the line says 'here, where you were begun, love begins again'. The Greek (exēgeirā se) and the Latin (suscitavi te) use a pronoun that is the same for either gender, so they do not decide (see the variant). The Latin Vulgate has a bleaker second half, 'there your mother was ruined' (corrupta est).
r: Song of Songs 2:3; Song of Songs 2:7; Genesis 2:9

a: Put me like a seal on your heart
t: The seal on the heart and arm
p: A seal is a personal mark worn on the chest or hand; it stands for ownership, closeness and identity.
b: The seal (chotam) was a stone stamp that a person used like a signature. It was carried on a cord around the neck, over the heart (Genesis 38:18, Judah's seal and cord), or on a ring on the hand (Jeremiah 22:24). The high priest bore the tribes' names on his heart and shoulders (Exodus 28:9–12, 29). To be set 'like a seal' on his heart and arm is to be close to what he feels and does, and marked as his. The New Testament speaks of believers 'sealed' with the Spirit (2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13), a different image that Christian readers have joined to this verse.
orig: שִׂימֵנִי כַחוֹתָם עַל לִבֶּךָ (simeni kachotam al libbekha)
r: Genesis 38:18; Jeremiah 22:24; Haggai 2:23; Exodus 28:29; 2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13

a: Because love is strong, like death
p: 'Azzah' is strong, fierce; the comparison with death is of its power to take, and not to be argued with.
b: Death takes everyone and can be neither bribed nor held back (Psalm 49:7–9; Ecclesiastes 8:8). Love is as strong: it takes a person and does not give back. The Hebrew says love is strong kammavet, 'as death', not 'stronger than death'. Christian readers sometimes read it as 'stronger' (Christ's love beating death), which the Hebrew does not say, though it fits the resurrection. Ahavah is 'love' here and in all other places in the Plain English Translation, never 'desire'. The line stands in parallel with 'jealousy is hard, like Sheol', and both are about the grip of love.
orig: כִּי עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה (ki azzah kammavet ahavah)
r: Psalm 49:7–9; Ecclesiastes 8:8; Proverbs 30:15–16

a: jealousy is hard, like Sheol
p: 'Qin'ah' covers jealousy, zeal and fierce loyalty; it is the word used of God's jealousy for his people.
b: Qin'ah means more than what English calls jealousy. It is the feeling that will not share what belongs to it: a husband's jealousy of his wife (Numbers 5:14; Proverbs 6:34), and God's jealousy for his people ('I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God', Exodus 20:5; Exodus 34:14; Deuteronomy 4:24). It can also be 'zeal', as when Phinehas was 'zealous with my zeal' (Numbers 25:11). Sheol is the underworld, the world of the dead, which never lets go. 'Hard' is qasheh, 'severe', and here means that the grip of love, like Sheol's, is not loosened. The Plain English Translation keeps 'jealousy' and the note says what it covers.
r: Exodus 20:5; Exodus 34:14; Numbers 5:14; Numbers 25:11; Proverbs 6:34; Deuteronomy 4:24

a: Its sparks are sparks of fire
p: 'Reshef' means a flash, a spark or a bolt of lightning; it is also the name of a Canaanite god of plague.
b: Reshef (plural reshafim) means a burning flash: lightning bolts in Psalm 78:48, sparks in Job 5:7, 'flashes of the bow' (arrows) in Psalm 76:3. The same word was the name of Resheph, a god of plague and war at Ugarit and in Egypt, and it is used of plague in Deuteronomy 32:24 and Habakkuk 3:5. Some scholars hear the god behind the word, but the Song is not worshiping him; the word means fiery flashes. The Plain English Translation says 'sparks', to avoid repeating 'flame' in the last phrase and to avoid 'bolts', which a reader could take for the door bolt of 5:5.
r: Psalm 78:48; Psalm 76:3; Deuteronomy 32:24; Habakkuk 3:5; Job 5:7

a: Yah
t: The one possible name of God
p: 'Shalhevetyah' may end with the divine name 'Yah', or the ending may only strengthen the word: 'a raging flame'.
b: Hebrew: shalhevetyah, 'a flame of Yah'. Yah is the short form of the LORD's name (Exodus 15:2; Psalm 118:5). If it is the divine name here, this is the only place in the Song that names God, and it would say that love's fire comes from him. If not, the ending -yah is a superlative, as in 'a great city to God' (Jonah 3:3) and 'a prince of God' (Genesis 23:6), so 'a mighty flame'. The Greek has just 'its flames', and the Latin has no name. Views by lens. H: the book otherwise avoids God's name, so a superlative is likely. L: scholars divide; Garrett defends the divine name, and others take 'Yah' as a superlative. J: the rabbis took it as God's name and read the verse as Israel's love for God. X: the Fathers took it as the Spirit's fire or Christ's love. M: readers such as Trible and Exum note that the Song never makes God its speaker or its subject, so a divine name here would be a rare touch.
r: Exodus 15:2; Jonah 3:3; Genesis 23:6; Psalm 118:5

a: Put me like a seal on your heart, / like a seal on your arm
p: How the history, love-poetry, Jewish, Christian and modern readings take the most quoted verses of the book.
b: H, history: the verses sound like a closing proverb of wisdom, which may be why they sit near the end; the seal and the flood images belong to everyday life. L, love poetry: a poem about the invincibility of love between two people; it is the nearest the Song comes to a statement of its theme (Fox, Exum, Garrett). J, Jewish: Israel's love for God endures exile, death and the flood of the nations (Song of Songs Rabbah; Targum). X, Christian: Christ's love for the Church, as strong as the death he died; the flame is the Spirit; the seal is baptism or the Spirit. M, modern and women's: love as mutual belonging that cannot be bought or owned; the speaker sets terms to her lover as an equal. The traditions card below sets the Christian views side by side.
r: Song of Songs 2:7; Song of Songs 8:7; Exodus 28:29

a: Many waters cannot put out love
p: 'Many waters' are the waters of chaos in the Psalms; love stands up to them as it does to death.
b: 'Many waters' (mayim rabbim) is a Hebrew name for the great waters of chaos and of danger (Psalm 29:3; Psalm 93:4; Psalm 144:7). God is stronger than they are (Psalm 93:4), and a person who passes through them is saved by the LORD (Isaiah 43:2). Love is compared with that power: floods and rivers cannot put out its fire, because it is stronger than the water that quenches every other fire. Together with death and Sheol (8:6), the waters make a list of what overruns every human thing. Rabbinic readers took the waters as the nations that threaten Israel; Christian readers, as the world's trials.
orig: מַיִם רַבִּים לֹא יוּכְלוּ לְכַבּוֹת אֶת הָאַהֲבָה
r: Psalm 29:3; Psalm 93:4; Psalm 144:7; Isaiah 43:2

a: If a man gave for love all the wealth in his house
p: Love is not for sale; any offer would be met with contempt.
b: The point is that love has no price. Anyone who offered his whole fortune to buy it would only be mocked. The verse sets love against wealth, as the end of the book will set the woman's own vineyard against Solomon's thousand (8:11–12). Proverbs 6:34–35 describes the jealous husband who will take no payment and no bribe to forgive the man who took his wife. In the Song the same unbending quality is the strength of love itself. The Hebrew uses an emphatic form (bouz yavuzu) to say 'they would utterly despise it'.
r: Proverbs 6:34–35; Song of Songs 8:11–12

a: We have a little sister
t: Who speaks of the little sister?
p: The speakers may be the brothers of 1:6, now discussing the woman as she was, or her younger sister.
b: Who is 'we', and who is the 'little sister'? Views. (1) The brothers of 1:6 speak about the woman when she was young: they were her guards (the wall and the door of 8:9), and 8:10 is her reply. (2) The speakers are her brothers, planning for a younger sister who has not yet matured, and the woman is the one who answers for her. (3) The speakers are the woman's friends or her family, and the sister is a third person in the story. Whoever speaks, the passage shows the family deciding a girl's future. 'On the day she is spoken about' may be the day a suitor asks for her, or the day she is accused.
r: Song of Songs 1:6; Genesis 24:50–60; Genesis 34:13–17

a: If she is a wall
p: The brothers plan: if she is a wall, they will crown her; if a door, they will bar her.
b: A wall is closed and firm; a door opens and swings. The brothers' plan has two cases. If she stays closed, they will add a battlement of silver on her wall, as a reward or an adornment. If she is open, they will board her up with cedar. Views. (1) A plan for her protection: reward chastity and block the risk of its loss. (2) A bargain: a silver battlement is a rich marriage settlement for a closed wall. (3) A pun: 'door' (delet) can also be a hinged board, so the cedar plank bars it shut. The woman answers at once with 'I am a wall'.
orig: אִם חוֹמָה הִיא נִבְנֶה עָלֶיהָ טִירַת כָּסֶף
r: Song of Songs 8:10; 1 Kings 6:15; Genesis 25:16

a: I am a wall, / and my breasts are like towers
p: She says she is already a wall with towers: grown up, self-guarded, and a source of peace.
b: The woman takes up the brothers' word 'wall' and says she is one, and that her breasts are towers. Views. (1) She is grown up (towers are breasts), and she has kept herself as a wall, so her brothers' plan is not needed. (2) She is saying 'I am my own fortress', and so refusing their control over her (compare 1:6). (3) The speaker is the 'little sister' of the brothers, now grown. The shift from 'she has no breasts' (8:8) to 'my breasts are like towers' is the story of her coming of age in two verses. The fortress image also looks ahead to the vineyard of 8:12: she has her own to keep.
r: Song of Songs 8:8; Song of Songs 8:12; Song of Songs 7:4

a: like one who finds peace
p: 'Shalom' (peace, wholeness) sounds like Shelomoh (Solomon), whose name opens the next verse.
b: Shalom is not only the absence of war, but wholeness and well-being. The woman says she became, in his eyes, 'one who finds shalom': one who receives welcome and favor, or one who comes to terms. The next verse begins with Shelomoh, 'Solomon', and the sound is the same root. So the line leads the ear from peace to Solomon. The Song's other word plays on the root include 'Shulammite' (6:13).
r: Song of Songs 6:13; Song of Songs 8:11

a: at Baal-hamon
p: Baal-hamon, 'owner of abundance', is not located; the Book of Judith mentions a Balamon near Dothan.
b: Ba'al-hamon means 'lord of a multitude' or 'owner of abundance'. No such place is known. Some link it with the Balamon of Judith 8:3 (near Dothan) and with Ibleam or Belmen in the northern hills; others take the name as symbolic, a place of great wealth or many workers. The Greek writes it as a name (Beethlamōn in Swete's Vaticanus). The crown held royal vineyards (1 Chronicles 27:27, under David; Ecclesiastes 2:4, where the king-speaker plants vineyards), but Baal-hamon is not named in either. The Plain English Translation gives the name as it stands.
r: Judith 8:3; 1 Chronicles 27:27; Ecclesiastes 2:4

a: Each man would bring in a thousand silver pieces for its fruit
p: Solomon leases his vineyard to tenants who pay a thousand pieces each; the woman will set her own vineyard against it.
b: A rich man's vineyard worked by tenant keepers is a picture of wealth and ownership. The tenants pay a thousand silver pieces for the fruit; Isaiah 7:23 gives the same figure (the Hebrew is the same, elef kesef; the Plain English Translation of Isaiah says 'a thousand pieces of silver') as the worth of a vineyard of a thousand vines. Views. (1) A plain business scene that sets up the contrast of 8:12. (2) Solomon's vineyard is his harem of wives (the 700 and 300 of 1 Kings 11:3), a place with many keepers. (3) The vineyard is Israel, leased out to rulers, as in Isaiah 5:1–7, and the 'keepers' are the kings and priests (Targum). The lines are in the third person, as though told as a story, and they lead to her reply.
r: Isaiah 7:23; Isaiah 5:1–7; 1 Kings 11:3; Matthew 21:33

a: My own vineyard is in front of me
p: The woman's own vineyard is hers to guard and give; this is the answer to 1:6.
b: 'Vineyard' has been her self since 1:6, when she said she had not guarded her own. Now it is 'in front of me': in her sight, under her own control, hers to keep or give. Solomon may keep his wealth and his tenants; she will not trade herself. This is the Song's final reply to the brothers, to Solomon and to the whole idea that love can be owned. Some feminist readers, such as Exum, read the line as the woman's declaration of independence. Longman reads it as faithfulness: she guards herself for one man.
r: Song of Songs 1:6; Song of Songs 2:15; Song of Songs 8:7

a: The thousand are yours, Solomon
p: The woman speaks to Solomon: he may keep his thousand; the keepers get their two hundred.
b: The woman turns to Solomon and calls him by name. Views. (1) She gives him his due, with irony: let him keep his wealth, her love is not part of it. (2) She really is the lover's partner, and Solomon is the lover, who may have his thousand while she keeps her own vineyard, a gift to be shared on her terms. (3) 'Solomon' stands for any man who thinks money can buy love (compare 8:7). (4) In the Targum and the rabbis, Solomon (Shelomoh, 'the king to whom peace belongs') is God, and the thousand and the two hundred are the offerings of Israel and the care of the keepers of the Law. The Song names Solomon seven times and this is the last.
r: 1 Kings 11:1–3; Ecclesiastes 2:8; Song of Songs 1:1; Song of Songs 3:11

a: You who live in the gardens
p: The man speaks to the woman, who sits in the gardens; the companions listen for her voice.
b: The word is feminine: 'you who live in the gardens' is the woman, and the speaker is the man, who has now come to her gardens. The 'companions' (chaverim) are listening for her voice. In 1:7 she did not want to be near his companions; now they stand by to hear her. He wants her to speak and sing: 'let me hear it', as in 2:14. Allegory takes the gardens as the Church or the synagogues, the companions as the angels or the disciples, and the voice as her prayer. Origen and the Targum both give it that sense.
r: Song of Songs 1:7; Song of Songs 2:14; Song of Songs 5:1

a: Hurry, my lover
p: The Song ends with 'hurry' or 'run away': a call to come or to go, read as longing for the Messiah or Christ's return.
b: Berach is literally 'run away, flee', as in Genesis 31:20; it can also mean 'hurry'. So the last line may be a call to come quickly, or to go quickly (as in 2:17, where she told him to turn and go until the day breathed). The gazelle and young deer, the mountains of spices, tie it to the book's start (2:9; 4:6). The Song ends open. Jewish readers took the line as Israel's prayer for the Messiah and God's return, and Christian readers as the prayer of the Church for Christ's return (compare the Aramaic Maranatha, 'Our Lord, come', in 1 Corinthians 16:22 and the closing prayer 'Come, Lord Jesus' in Revelation 22:20, an echo and not a quotation). The Targum has Israel pray in exile that God would hasten to redeem her.
r: Genesis 31:20; Song of Songs 2:17; Revelation 22:20; 1 Corinthians 16:22
